source_refs.note: Topic 6.2, printed pages 119-120 (Figure 6.2), with Quick Check 6.1 as the self-check.

blocks.text: All chemical reactions involve the breaking of bonds in the reactant molecules before the formation of new bonds. This can be achieved only if the reactant molecules collide with sufficient amount of energy to overcome an energy barrier. This minimum amount of energy required by the reactant molecules just to cross that energy barrier is called energy of activation denoted by Ea. The energy profile diagram of exothermic and endothermic reactions are given in Figure 6.2.

blocks.alt: Two energy profiles, Enthalpy against Progress of Reaction. Left (exothermic): a red curve rises from the reactants level HR to a peak and falls to the lower products level HP; a dashed arrow Ea goes from HR up to the peak and a solid arrow delta H goes from HR down to HP. Right (endothermic): the curve rises from HR (reactants, low) to a peak and falls to HP (products, higher); a dashed arrow Ea from HR to the peak and an arrow delta H from HR up to HP.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.2: Energy profile diagram in terms of ΔH and Ea (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.2).

blocks.prompt:
Draw the energy profile diagrams for the following reactions:
i. CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l)    ΔH = –890.3 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.explanation: Draw the reactants line high. The curve rises to a hump (Ea) and then falls 890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ to the lower products line. This is an exothermic profile.

answer_figure.alt: Energy profile for burning methane: enthalpy (y-axis) against progress of reaction. The reactants line CH₄ + 2O₂ (HR) is high; the red curve rises to a hump (Ea, dashed arrow from the reactants to the peak), then falls to the products line CO₂ + 2H₂O(l) (HP). Downward arrow from HR to HP: ΔH = −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic).
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: exothermic energy profile of CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹
answer_figure.long_description: On the left the reactants line CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) is high (HR) and on the right the products line CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) is low (HP). In between, the curve forms a hump (the energy barrier); the dashed arrow from the reactants level to the peak is the activation energy Ea. The downward arrow from HR to HP shows ΔH = −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹: the products have a lower enthalpy, so heat is released.

blocks.prompt: ii. CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)    ΔH = +572 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.explanation: Draw the reactant line low. The curve passes over a hump (Ea) and ends on the products line, 572 kJ mol⁻¹ higher. This is an endothermic profile; Ea must be at least as large as ΔH (572 kJ mol⁻¹). (The accepted value of ΔH is about +178 kJ mol⁻¹; see the Book correction. The shape of the diagram is the same.)

answer_figure.alt: Energy profile for the decomposition of calcium carbonate: the reactant line CaCO₃ (HR) is low; the red curve passes over a hump (Ea) and ends on the higher products line CaO + CO₂ (HP). Upward arrow from HR to HP: ΔH = +572 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic, the book's value).
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: endothermic energy profile of CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ with the book's value ΔH = +572 kJ mol⁻¹ (the accepted value is about +178 kJ mol⁻¹)
answer_figure.long_description: On the left the reactant line CaCO₃(s) is low (HR) and on the right the products line CaO(s) + CO₂(g) is high (HP). The curve passes over a hump; the dashed arrow from HR to the peak is Ea, which is larger than ΔH. The upward arrow from HR to HP is ΔH = +572 kJ mol⁻¹ (the book's value): the products have a higher enthalpy, so heat is absorbed. Data tables give about +178 kJ mol⁻¹ for this reaction; the shape stays the same.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The enthalpy change for CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) is printed as +572 kJ mol⁻¹. The accepted value is about +178 kJ mol⁻¹; the reaction is endothermic either way.
